Project1.Title: MuscleMate (In Progress)
Project1.Desc: MuscleMate is a fitness-tracking app for intermediate and advanced lifters. It features customizable workout logging, a workout history to view past workouts, progress tracking for key lifts, and a coach view where coaches can monitor clients' progress. The app avoids unnecessary pre-made templates and form tutorials, focusing instead on user customization.

Project2.Title: TripSplit (October 2025 - June 2026)
Project2.Desc: TripSplit is a cross-platform iOS/Android mobile app for splitting expenses on group trips. Built with React Native (Expo) on the front end and a Node.js/Express backend with a PostgreSQL database, it lets travelers create a trip, invite friends, log expenses with itemized splits, scan paper receipts with the camera (OCR + AI parsing), settle up via Venmo/Cash App/PayPal deep links, and track who owes whom in real time. Think Splitwise, but built around an actual trip with currency conversion, push notifications, and a tighter payment confirmation flow.
Project2.RepoNote: Source repository kept private: available on request.

Extended.Purpose: TripSplit was inspired by the frustration of managing shared expenses during group travel. Splitting costs usually meant manually tracking receipts, calculating balances, and sorting out payments afterward, so I wanted to create a smoother experience that handled those steps in one place. The project also pushed me technically because it was the first time I built and connected a complete full-stack system, including the frontend, backend, database, authentication, OCR integration, and deployment.

items: Expo Router (file-based routing), Expo Image Picker, Expo Image Manipulator, Expo Notifications, Expo Constants
Firebase Authentication (email/password, email verification, persistent sessions via AsyncStorage)
React Navigation, React Native Gesture Handler
Firebase Admin SDK for token verification
Resend for transactional email (verification, password reset)
A local Ollama LLM (llama3.1) called via an HTTP adapter to parse OCR'd receipt text into structured expense data (merchant, line items, tax, tip, total, currency)
JWT, bcrypt, and Zod for validation
Docker Compose for local dev (Postgres + API + ngrok + Expo)
AWS Elastic Beanstalk for production deployment, Let's Encrypt for HTTPS
EAS Build for iOS dev/release builds

Lessons: Building TripSplit taught me how much coordination goes into a real full-stack application beyond just writing frontend code. I learned how to design APIs, structure and connect a database, handle authentication and state management, debug issues across multiple systems, and integrate external services like OCR for receipt scanning. It also gave me experience thinking about usability and edge cases, since small details in expense splitting and payment flows had a big impact on the user experience.

The project also helped me become more comfortable working in a team environment. I collaborated through Git and pull requests, worked across shared codebases, participated in testing and demos, and learned how to balance technical decisions with deadlines and MVP scope. It was the first project where I felt like I was building something that resembled a real production application instead of just a class assignment.

TeamLessons.title: Branch hygiene matters
TeamLessons.body: Working on a long-lived feature branch while teammates also pushed to main meant repeated merges. I learned to pull main often, resolve conflicts in small chunks rather than mega-merges, and document Mac-local config (Dockerfile tweaks, package.json deltas) that should not be pushed.

TeamLessons.title: Async coordination via commits
TeamLessons.body: With no real-time pair programming, the commit message was the handoff. Clear, scoped commits like 'fix: trip add-member optimistic Invited pill + per-row spinner; no full reload' told my teammate exactly what changed without needing a meeting.

KnownIssues: iOS receipt crop is locked to a square. Apple's native UIImagePickerController doesn't support non-square crop areas, so tall receipts get cut off. Working around this requires either a third-party native library (react-native-image-crop-picker) or a custom JS crop screen.
Email service is fragile. The Resend client is instantiated at module load, so if RESEND_API_KEY is missing the entire backend crashes on boot instead of degrading gracefully.
We don’t have many automated tests.
OCR + LLM accuracy varies. Long receipts, dim lighting, and non-USD currencies all degrade results.
Improvements: Replace Expo's image picker with react-native-image-crop-picker for proper 4-corner freeform crop on receipts (both platforms).
Add a real test suite: Jest for backend, React Native Testing Library for components.
Make the email service lazy-init so a missing API key warns instead of crashing.
Apple Pay functionality alongside the existing Venmo / Cash App / PayPal options.
Server-side receipt-image storage (currently the photo is OCR'd locally and only the text is sent, so saving the image would let users review original receipts later).

Project3.Title: Go Syntax Parser & Lexical Analyzer
Project3.Desc: A full compiler front-end project written in Go, built for my Programming Languages course. Using a custom grammar, I implemented a full lexical analyzer, and built a recursive-descent parser capable of validating and analyzing programs. This project required designing tokens, building a symbol table, handling errors cleanly, and producing structured parse output. It helped deepen my understanding of compiler design, lexing, parsing, and language theory.

Project4.Title: Desegregating Schools - Data Analytics Project
Project4.Desc: Desegregating Schools: Charlotte & Seattle is a data science project examining how school diversity relates to neighborhood rent levels in Seattle and Charlotte. Our team combined public school enrollment data, census variables, GIS shapefiles, and rent datasets to analyze spatial patterns of segregation and housing affordability. I led the Seattle data work, including cleaning enrollment data, creating a school-to-neighborhood matching table, merging spatial files, and producing the Seattle scatterplot showing the relationship between rent and percent students of color. As a team, we built maps, scatterplots, and an interactive Shiny app using R (ggplot2, sf, tmap, leaflet) to compare citywide trends. Our findings show clear disparities: schools in higher-rent neighborhoods tend to enroll fewer students of color, while more affordable areas are significantly more diverse. The project highlights how housing patterns and gentrification continue to shape educational equity.
